title: Nehemiah 4:7–23
context: As the gaps in the wall close, Sanballat, Tobiah, and their allies conspire to attack Jerusalem. The builders pray and set a watch day and night, Nehemiah arms the people by families and urges them to remember the Lord, and God brings the enemies’ plan to nothing. From then on half work while half stand guard, the builders keep weapons at hand, and a trumpet signal is ready, with the assurance “Our God will fight for us.” Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about prayer and watchfulness, human means and God’s protection.

verses.text: But when Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites heard that the repairing of the walls of Jerusalem went forward, and that the breaches began to be filled, they were very angry;
verses.arminianNotes:
When Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabians, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites hear that the repairs are progressing and the gaps closing, they become very angry. Opposition surrounds the city.

Arminian readers see hostility growing as the work advances.
verses.reformedNotes:
The list of opponents suggests pressure from several directions, though the exact political arrangements are not described.

Reformed readers see the work of God provoking wider resistance. Both traditions read this as shared ground and keep historical reconstruction tentative.

verses.text: and they all conspired together to come and fight against Jerusalem, and to cause confusion among us.
verses.arminianNotes:
They all conspire to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion. Mockery turns to plotting.

Arminian readers see a coordinated, deliberate choice to stop the work by force and by spreading fear and disorder among the builders.
verses.reformedNotes:
The aim of causing confusion shows that fear and disorder were weapons alongside force.

Reformed readers see enemies plotting against God’s purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the reality of opposition to God’s work and the threat it posed to the builders.

verses.text: But we made our prayer to our God, and set a watch against them day and night because of them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But we made our prayer to our God, and set a watch against them day and night.” Prayer and watchfulness stand together.

Arminian readers see trust in God expressed alongside responsible action.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse joins dependence on God with practical defense, and neither replaces the other. Whether prayer changes what God does is treated at the Joshua 10:14 box.

Reformed readers see God working through means. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground.

verses.text: Judah said, “The strength of the bearers of burdens is fading and there is much rubble, so that we are not able to build the wall.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Judah says the strength of the burden bearers is failing and the rubble is great, so they cannot build. Discouragement arises within.

Arminian readers see real weariness that threatens to stop the work, an honest picture of human limits.
verses.reformedNotes:
The complaint comes from Judah itself, not from the enemy, showing that exhaustion can be as dangerous as opposition.

Reformed readers see God’s people needing strength beyond their own. Both traditions read this as shared ground about weariness in faithful work and the need for encouragement.

verses.text: Our adversaries said, “They will not know or see, until we come in among them and kill them, and cause the work to cease.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The adversaries plan to come in among them unseen, kill them, and stop the work. The threat is deadly.

Arminian readers see enemies freely choosing violence and secrecy to defeat God’s people and halt the building.
verses.reformedNotes:
The plan relies on surprise. Nehemiah’s response in the following verses will remove that advantage.

Reformed readers see God’s people under real threat. Both traditions read this as shared ground and see the narrative moving from threat to God’s deliverance through watchfulness and courage.

verses.text: When the Jews who lived by them came, they said to us ten times from all places, “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jews living near the enemies come and warn them ten times from every direction that the enemies will attack wherever they turn. Warnings multiply.

Arminian readers see information that calls for a response.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘ten times’ likely means repeatedly rather than an exact count. The exact sense of the warning’s wording is debated, but its urgency is clear.

Reformed readers see God providing warning through his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground about heeding warnings.

verses.text: Therefore I set guards in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in the open places. I set the people by family groups with their swords, their spears, and their bows.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah stations people behind the wall at its lowest, most exposed points, by families, with swords, spears, and bows. Defense is organized.

Arminian readers see wise leadership responding to danger.
verses.reformedNotes:
Placing families together gave each defender a personal stake in the defense.

Reformed readers see God protecting his people through ordinary means. Both traditions read this as shared ground about prudent action joined to trust in God, without treating the arming of the people as a contradiction of faith.

verses.text: I looked, and rose up, and said to the nobles, to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, “Don’t be afraid of them! Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your houses.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah tells the nobles, rulers, and people not to be afraid, but to remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and to fight for their families and houses. Faith answers fear.

Arminian readers see courage grounded in remembering God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Nehemiah’s appeal joins confidence in God’s greatness with responsibility for those at home.

Reformed readers see fear overcome by a right view of God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about courage rooted in who God is.

verses.text: When our enemies heard that it was known to us, and God had brought their counsel to nothing, all of us returned to the wall, everyone to his work.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the enemies learn that their plot is known and that God has brought their counsel to nothing, everyone returns to the wall and his work. The plot fails.

Arminian readers see God frustrating hostile plans while the builders act responsibly.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator credits God with defeating the plan; how God governs hostile agents is treated at Judges 9:23.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign protection of his work. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both note the quiet return to ordinary work.

verses.text: From that time forth, half of my servants did the work, and half of them held the spears, the shields, the bows, and the coats of mail; and the rulers were behind all the house of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
From then on, half of Nehemiah’s servants work while half hold spears, shields, bows, and armor, and the leaders stand behind the people of Judah. Work and watch are shared.

Arminian readers see sustained watchfulness without abandoning the work.
verses.reformedNotes:
The arrangement continues the pattern of verse 9: labor and defense together.

Reformed readers see leaders supporting those who work. Both traditions read this as shared ground about vigilance and diligence held together over time.

verses.text: Those who built the wall, and those who bore burdens loaded themselves; everyone with one of his hands did the work, and with the other held his weapon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Those who build and those who carry burdens work with one hand and hold a weapon with the other. Readiness marks the work.

Arminian readers see the image as a vivid picture of the watchfulness that the people chose to maintain while building.
verses.reformedNotes:
Interpreters differ on how literally to picture the arrangement, but the point of constant readiness is plain.

Reformed readers see constant readiness. Both traditions read this as shared ground and do not press the details.

verses.text: Among the builders, everyone wore his sword at his side, and so built. He who sounded the trumpet was by me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Each builder wears his sword at his side as he builds, and the trumpeter stays beside Nehemiah. Communication is prepared.

Arminian readers see practical planning that lets the scattered builders respond together when danger comes.
verses.reformedNotes:
The trumpeter beside Nehemiah prepares for the signal described in verses 19–20.

Reformed readers see order and readiness in God’s work. Both traditions read this as shared ground about wise preparation and the leader’s responsibility to coordinate the people.

verses.text: I said to the nobles, and to the rulers and to the rest of the people, “The work is great and widely spread out, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah tells the leaders and people that the work is great and widely spread, and they are separated far from one another on the wall. Distance creates danger.

Arminian readers see a leader honestly naming the risk and explaining the plan.
verses.reformedNotes:
The spread-out work made the builders vulnerable to attack at any single point.

Reformed readers see wisdom in addressing the people’s situation openly. Both traditions read this as shared ground about leadership that explains the danger and calls the community to act together.

verses.text: Wherever you hear the sound of the trumpet, rally there to us. Our God will fight for us.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wherever they hear the trumpet, they are to rally there, and “Our God will fight for us.” Confidence rests in God.

Arminian readers see trust in God motivating the people’s ready response.
verses.reformedNotes:
The words recall earlier assurances that God fights for his people, while the rally plan remains in place.

Reformed readers see God as the defender of his people working through their obedience. Both traditions read this as shared ground about trust and action joined together.

verses.text: So we did the work. Half of the people held the spears from the rising of the morning until the stars appeared.
verses.arminianNotes:
So they work, with half holding spears from dawn until the stars appear. The labor is long.

Arminian readers see persevering effort sustained over many long days, as the people keep both their work and their watch.
verses.reformedNotes:
The time markers stress how demanding the work was.

Reformed readers see God sustaining his people through toil. Both traditions read this as shared ground about faithful endurance in God’s work, with watchfulness and labor continuing together from morning until night.

verses.text: Likewise at the same time I said to the people, “Let everyone with his servant lodge within Jerusalem, that in the night they may be a guard to us, and may labor in the day.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah tells everyone to lodge within Jerusalem with his servant, so they can guard by night and labor by day. Rest is reorganized.

Arminian readers see sacrifice willingly accepted for the common good.
verses.reformedNotes:
Staying in the city removed the danger of travel at night and added defenders.

Reformed readers see wise provision for the community’s safety. Both traditions read this as shared ground about practical care and the readiness of God’s people to give up comfort for a shared task.

verses.text: So neither I, nor my brothers, nor my servants, nor the men of the guard who followed me took off our clothes. Everyone took his weapon to the water.
verses.arminianNotes:
Neither Nehemiah, his brothers, his servants, nor the guard take off their clothes, and each takes his weapon even to the water. Vigilance is constant.

Arminian readers see a leader sharing the people’s hardships.
verses.reformedNotes:
The final clause is difficult, and translations render it in different ways; its general sense of constant readiness is clear.

Reformed readers see an example of tireless service. Both traditions read this as shared ground about leaders who share the burden.
